weekly.2026-08-03:
Week six opened with Trump's promised Monday talks still unstarted and Tehran denying any were happening. The Pentagon had burned through nearly 80% of its THAAD interceptors, Netanyahu rejected the Hamas disarmament draft, and the UN said Iran has executed at least 56 people since March. Trump gave his most direct Hormuz ultimatum yet — 'open very soon, or they're going to get hit very hard.'

The back half exposed how thin that optimism was. Trump, furious at reports the interceptor stockpile had cratered, vowed to jail the 'leakers' — then quietly gave contractors 21 days to plan faster munitions output. Vance called Iran a 'fractured system' where talks will be 'messy'; Gen. Dan Caine privately told Trump's circle the US needs an 'off-ramp.' Hormuz diplomacy inched forward on paper as Iran and Oman neared a split-lane framework, but Tehran then attached six formal conditions — US withdrawal, reparations, an end to the blockade — that one analyst called ones 'the US cannot accept,' and an Iranian missile struck a UAE tanker in the strait. By Sunday Iran had handed the file to former IRGC commander Mohsen Rezaei as security council chief, and Trump had stopped pretending: 'We are only semi-negotiating with them.'

The periphery widened regardless. Houthi missiles killed 58 Yemeni troops, wounded 11 in Najran, hit Aramco's Jizan refinery, then killed 7 more at Mokha port. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed the Mecca mutual-defense pact. Israeli troops built an earthen barrier inside a Lebanese army-held village even as Beirut and Jerusalem agreed a shortlist of disarmament verifiers — the week's one concrete step, in a war its own architects admit has no clean end.
weekly.2026-06-22:
The week opened with the implementation deal producing machinery instead of signatures and ended with that machinery battered but not abandoned. After an 18-hour Switzerland marathon, Vance claimed four wins — IAEA readmission, a Hormuz mechanism, a Lebanon deconfliction cell and a structure for talks — and dividends piled up: a 60-day Treasury oil license, Tehran's claimed $12bn frozen-funds release, an Oman-IMO corridor evacuating 11,000+ stranded seafarers, a reopened US embassy in Kuwait, and oil falling below its pre-war level (Brent near $72) as Qatar pledged near-normal LNG within weeks.

Then the choke point reignited. IRGC drones hit the Ever Lovely off Oman (June 25) and the tanker Kiku (June 27); the US answered with two straight nights of strikes near Sirik as Trump threatened to 'complete the job,' and on June 28 Iran fired missiles and drones at US bases in Kuwait and Bahrain — mostly intercepted, but a Bahrain home was damaged and a Qatari civilian killed by shrapnel. Both sides briefly declared the diplomacy dead before reversing course the same day: they agreed to stand down, reopened Hormuz to traffic, and Pakistan said talks would resume Tuesday — confirming the war's rhythm of escalation snapping back to the table.

Lebanon tracked a grimmer arc. Israel, Lebanon and the US signed a June 26 framework for a token IDF pullback, which Netanyahu cast as license to hold most of the south and Hezbollah rejected outright; within a day Israeli strikes killed at least 27 there, and by June 28 a Hezbollah gunman had killed an Israeli officer in Deir Siryan — the first fatality since the deal — as the IDF kept demolishing tunnels.
weekly.2026-02-23: Week 1 was the week the war began — and immediately became something larger than anyone publicly planned for. The US-Israeli opening salvo was devastating in its precision (Khamenei killed, 900+ targets hit in 12 hours), but Iran's instantaneous retaliation against all six GCC states revealed the fatal flaw in the 'surgical strike' theory: there was no version of this war that stayed contained. By week's end, Hezbollah had opened a second front from Lebanon, the Strait of Hormuz was under threat, oil was climbing past $80, and the Kuwaiti friendly-fire incident had exposed the chaos of Gulf airspace. The most telling detail was the Omani foreign minister's revelation that Iran had agreed to zero enrichment hours before the bombs fell — a diplomatic breakthrough destroyed by the war it was meant to prevent. The week ended with Iran forming an Interim Leadership Council, signaling continuity of command rather than collapse, and the Western alliance already fracturing over the question of participation versus condemnation.
weekly.2026-03-02: The second week was when the war's geographic and economic dimensions exploded beyond any containment. Iran's formal closure of the Strait of Hormuz on March 4 turned a military conflict into a global economic crisis — Brent crude blew past $120 and the world lost access to 20% of its daily oil supply. The conflict's footprint stretched from the Caucasus (Iran striking Azerbaijan) to the Indian Ocean (the USS Charlotte sinking an Iranian frigate off Sri Lanka), proving this was no longer a regional war. Domestically, each side hardened: Mojtaba Khamenei's election as supreme leader elevated Iran's most radical faction, while Trump's emergency $650M arms sale bypassing Congress showed Washington preparing for a long campaign. The humanitarian toll became impossible to ignore — the UN declared 3.2 million Iranians displaced, and Macron's fury over UNIFIL casualties marked the moment European solidarity with the US began to crack. Israel's strikes on Iranian oil infrastructure, the Shahed drone factory in Isfahan, and IRGC commanders in Beirut showed a campaign methodically dismantling Iran's military-industrial base, its proxy command structure, and its economic lifeline simultaneously. Bahrain's desalination plant strike crossed a humanitarian threshold that even war-hardened observers found alarming.
weekly.2026-03-09: Week 3 was defined by the race between military destruction and diplomatic reality. The US and Israel were systematically dismantling Iran's nuclear and missile infrastructure — Parchin, Natanz (re-struck with bunker-busters), Kharg Island's oil terminal, and 200+ targets across three cities in a single day — while claiming 90% degradation of Iran's missile capability. But the IEA's declaration of the 'largest oil supply disruption in history' made clear the economic damage was already irreversible regardless of military outcomes. NATO's formal rejection of Trump's call for support was the week's political watershed — the alliance that had invoked Article 5 for Afghanistan wouldn't fight for Iran, leaving the US with only Israel at its side. The death of a French soldier near Erbil raised the specter of NATO being dragged in anyway, through the back door of individual-country casualties. Lebanon's President Aoun calling for direct talks with Israel and France proposing a ceasefire plan showed the diplomatic track trying to separate Lebanon from the broader conflict. Iran's mining of the Strait of Hormuz forced a naval minesweeping campaign that would take months regardless of how the war ended — a slow-burning consequence that would outlast any ceasefire.
weekly.2026-03-16: The war's fourth week saw the conflict metastasize in every direction simultaneously. Israel launched a full ground invasion of Lebanon while striking Iranian naval targets in the Caspian Sea — shattering geographic containment and forcing Russia to confront Israeli operations near its borders. Iran fired 19 attack waves at Israel in a single day, proving that claims of 90% missile degradation were premature. Trump's administration became openly contradictory: lifting Iranian oil sanctions to calm markets while deploying 2,500 more Marines; hinting at 'winding down' while the Pentagon considered occupying Kharg Island. The $200 billion supplemental budget request revealed the war's true cost, and strikes on South Pars — the world's largest gas field, shared with Qatar — risked turning Gulf energy partners into adversaries. The week's strategic pivot was Trump's 48-hour ultimatum to destroy Iran's power grid, the most explicit threat of collective punishment yet. The Dimona strike (180 wounded near Israel's nuclear reactor) showed Iran was mirror-imaging Israeli targeting doctrine. Lebanon's PM Salam openly accused the IRGC of commanding Hezbollah operations from Lebanese soil — the clearest sign yet that the 'axis of resistance' was fracturing under the weight of a war that was destroying the countries it was supposed to protect.
weekly.2026-03-23:
The war's first month ended with diplomacy and destruction racing each other. Trump's 5-day energy strike pause was the first real de-escalation — but the same week brought the Bushehr nuclear plant strike, the closest brush with radiological disaster, and the Houthis entering the war with missiles aimed at Israel. Pakistan emerged as the central mediator, hosting a four-nation summit in Islamabad, while Lebanon expelled Iran's ambassador in the sharpest break yet from the 'axis of resistance.'

On the battlefield, both sides widened their target sets past any remaining red lines. Israel blacked out Tehran by hitting the power grid; Iran struck aluminium smelters in the UAE and Bahrain, and pounded Kuwait's civilian infrastructure. Iran's selective Hormuz opening — letting Chinese, Russian, and Pakistani ships through while blocking Western vessels — weaponized shipping lanes along geopolitical fault lines. Brent crude hit $115.93, up 62% since the war began.

The week's defining contradiction: Trump claiming Iran had agreed to 'most of' his 15-point peace plan while telling the Financial Times he wanted to 'take the oil in Iran.' By week's end the IFRC had verified 1,900 Iranian dead, and the war was widening on every axis.
weekly.2026-03-30:
Week 5 shattered multiple frameworks simultaneously. Iran shot down two US aircraft in one day — an F-15E and an A-10 — the first American combat losses in the conflict. The subsequent deep-Iran rescue of the missing WSO, involving a CIA deception campaign and dozens of special forces, was the week's most operationally audacious event and the first clear US success in the land domain.

Economic warfare hit civilian thresholds no one had modeled. The Iran-Oman Hormuz protocol formalized a $2M-per-transit toll booth; France's CMA CGM made the first Western vessel crossing; EU diesel prices surged 30%+ as Commissioner Jorgensen warned of a 'long crisis.' Iran's execution of 18-year-old protester Amirhossein Hatami, and the IDF's return to Litani River positions showed both sides using wartime emergency to institutionalize control. Gulf states bore escalating punishment: Iran's largest single-day UAE barrage (23 missiles + 56 UAVs), then 60 more projectiles at the UAE on Easter Sunday; Kuwait's desalination plants hit repeatedly, threatening 90% of its drinking water; Bahrain's oil storage struck. Israeli Easter Sunday strikes killed 11 across Lebanon including a 4-year-old child.

Trump's 48-hour Hormuz ultimatum and the Mahshahr petrochemical strike (5 killed, 170 injured) compressed the week into a countdown toward April 6 — a deadline that arrived and was promptly extended to Tuesday, ensuring the trip wire stayed live.
weekly.2026-04-06:
Week 6 compressed the war's entire arc into nine days: civilizational threat, ceasefire, immediate fracturing, the highest-level US-Iran diplomacy since 1979, its collapse, a naval blockade, and a frantic multilateral scramble to prevent the truce from dying. Pakistan brokered the ceasefire 90 minutes before Trump's deadline. Oil plunged 14-16% — then reversed course entirely as the deal unraveled.

The ceasefire fractured from day one. Israel launched 'Operation Eternal Darkness' (303 killed in Lebanon's deadliest day), rejected any Hezbollah ceasefire, and kept hitting southern Lebanon — pushing the toll past 2,089. The IDF encircled Bint Jbeil, claiming 100+ Hezbollah killed. After 21 hours of Islamabad talks collapsed over nuclear demands, Trump announced a naval blockade of Iranian ports; Iran branded it 'piracy.' Oil surged 7-8%, erasing the ceasefire rally. But by Monday, Trump claimed Iran had 'reached out' to resume talks, and crude retreated from its highs.

The week's defining feature was the emergence of parallel diplomatic tracks. France and the UK announced a 15+ nation defensive Hormuz escort mission. China and Pakistan unveiled a joint 5-point ceasefire initiative. Lavrov told Araghchi the conflict has 'no military solution.' Israel and Lebanon announced their first-ever direct talks for April 15 in Washington — though they disagreed on whether to discuss ceasefire or peace. Pakistani, Egyptian, and Turkish mediators launched shuttle diplomacy to bridge gaps before the April 21 expiry. The ceasefire survived its first week, but barely.
weekly.2026-04-13:
Week 7 compressed the war's central paradox into seven days: every de-escalation was immediately reversed, yet neither side moved to resume full-scale fighting. The Hormuz whipsaw was the defining sequence — Araghchi declared the strait 'completely open,' oil crashed 11-12%, then the IRGC reversed him within 24 hours and gunboats fired on an Indian tanker. India summoned Iran's ambassador — the first major non-belligerent diplomatic protest. The SNSC formalized Iran's position: Hormuz stays under military control until the war definitively ends. Oil surged back toward $98, erasing the crash entirely.

The Lebanon ceasefire frayed from its first minutes. Artillery hit Khiam within 30 minutes of the truce; a French UNIFIL soldier was killed in a Hezbollah-attributed ambush; an IDF soldier photographed smashing a Jesus statue in a Maronite village went viral with 5 million views. By Day 51, the IDF was conducting acknowledged strikes on Hezbollah positions despite Trump declaring Israel 'PROHIBITED' from bombing Lebanon.

The week ended in confrontation. The USS Spruance fired on and seized the Iranian cargo ship Touska — the first US attack on a merchant vessel — after a 6-hour standoff. Trump threatened to 'blow up' the entire country while dispatching Vance to Islamabad for Monday talks. Ghalibaf declared Iran 'far from the final discussion,' and Iran's official death toll reached 3,468. Macron and Starmer launched a 51-nation Hormuz naval initiative. With two days until the ceasefire expires, every layer of the conflict was actively deteriorating.
weekly.2026-04-20:
The week that was supposed to end the ceasefire instead produced its indefinite extension — then proved the truce was a framework for managed escalation, not peace. Iran rejected Islamabad talks, Trump reversed his 'highly unlikely' stance to grant an open-ended truce, and the IRGC answered by attacking three ships in Hormuz and seizing two. The US retaliated globally, seizing the supertanker M/T Majestic X in the Indian Ocean. Treasury's 'Economic Fury' sanctioned China's Hengli refinery, ~40 shipping companies, and froze $344M in crypto — the war's largest single-day enforcement action.

The third round of talks collapsed before it began — Trump cancelled Witkoff and Kushner's Pakistan trip, and Pezeshkian declared Iran won't negotiate 'under siege.' But by Sunday, Iran conveyed a new proposal through four mediators offering to reopen Hormuz with nuclear talks deferred — the first decoupling of the two files. Rubio immediately dismissed it as 'unacceptable,' insisting Iran can't retain control of the strait. Germany's Merz called the US 'humiliated' by Iran, comparing the war to Afghanistan — the sharpest European rebuke yet. Putin praised Iran's 'courage' as Araghchi arrived in St. Petersburg. At the UN, Guterres demanded the Security Council act: 'Open the Strait. No tolls. No discrimination. Let the global economy breathe.' By Day 60, Kpler quantified the blockade's pressure: Iran has 12-22 days of oil storage left, exports have collapsed 70%, and no tanker has evaded the US cordon. Mid-May production shutdowns now look inevitable.

Lebanon fractured visibly: Hezbollah killed IDF Sgt. Idan Fooks — the first direct truce combat death — then wounded two more soldiers by drone within 48 hours. Israel struck the Beqaa Valley for the first time in three weeks, killing 14. Hezbollah's Qassem called Israel talks a 'grave sin'; President Aoun fired back that war was the real 'treason.' Bennett and Lapid merged parties to challenge Netanyahu. Iran banned steel exports after strikes destroyed 25-30% of capacity and hanged its 8th protest detainee.
weekly.2026-05-11:
Week 11 was defined by the widening gap between diplomatic progress and battlefield reality. The 45-day Lebanon ceasefire extension and planned May 29 Pentagon talks gave the appearance of a peace track — but Israel struck 24+ villages the next day, and Lebanon's death toll crossed 3,000. Hezbollah launched its first drone swarm at a named Israeli installation while the IRGC claimed a total Hormuz blockade. A drone hit the UAE's Barakah nuclear plant — the first targeting of civilian nuclear infrastructure in the war. Iran formally rejected the US five-point proposal as 'surrender,' and Trump scheduled a Situation Room meeting to discuss renewed military options.

The week's revelations reshaped the war's narrative. The NYT disclosed two covert Israeli military bases in Iraq's desert, built before the war to support air operations against Iran — a sovereignty violation that killed a Bedouin shepherd and provoked Iraqi diplomatic protests. Israel seized 39 boats from a 426-person Gaza flotilla off Cyprus, with Turkey calling it 'piracy.' Iran's judiciary confirmed 39 wartime executions, accelerating the regime's domestic crackdown under cover of external conflict. The week ended with Trump canceling Monday's planned strike at Gulf allies' request, signaling that Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE — the war's reluctant participants — had emerged as the critical restraining force on American escalation.
weekly.2026-05-04:
The week opened with escalation and pivoted to the most concrete peace framework since the war began — then watched Iran reject its core terms while the naval war intensified, the IRGC issued its most explicit combat threats of the ceasefire, and diplomacy scrambled to find a second channel. Project Freedom launched Monday with 15,000 service members; Iran responded with missiles at the UAE. By Tuesday the operation was paused, Rubio declared Epic Fury 'over,' and a 14-point MOU neared completion. Wednesday's naval combat — Iranian forces attacking three US destroyers, CENTCOM striking three ports — proved the Strait remains an active warzone. Israel killed Radwan Force commander Balout in Beirut's first strike since the April ceasefire.

By Thursday Iran had declared enrichment 'non-negotiable,' calling the US proposal a 'wish-list.' The blockade tightened: four Iranian tankers disabled, 70+ vessels trapped worth $13 billion. Friday brought Trump's 'Project Freedom Plus' threat, a CIA assessment that Iran could endure the blockade four months, and 31+ killed in Lebanon. Saturday the IRGC declared missiles 'locked onto American targets' while Kuwait and the UAE intercepted more Iranian drones. Satellite imagery revealed a 52 km² oil slick off Kharg Island. On Sunday, Iran finally transmitted its counter-proposal through Pakistan — demanding Hormuz sovereignty, war compensation, and sanctions relief while omitting any nuclear concession. Trump rejected it as 'TOTALLY UNACCEPTABLE.' A drone hit a cargo ship in Qatari waters near Mesaieed. Sen. Kelly disclosed the US had expended 45% of precision missiles and 50%+ of THAAD interceptors; Hegseth threatened an investigation.

The week's paradox: Qatar's PM shuttled between Vance, Rubio, and Witkoff, declaring a 'high probability' of a deal, and the first Qatari LNG tanker since the war began transited Hormuz with Iranian approval — yet by week's end Iran had rejected the deal's nuclear terms, maximized its military rhetoric, and the diplomatic gap looked wider than when the week began. The $50 billion war's sustainability was publicly questioned for the first time by a US senator citing classified munitions data.
weekly.2026-04-27:
Week 9 crystallized the war's emerging endgame: a grinding economic siege punctuated by constitutional crisis, NATO fracture, and the war's first major civilian-sector casualty — then on Sunday, a direct military challenge to Iran's Hormuz control. Trump's 'Project Freedom' announcement — 15,000 service members, destroyers, and 100+ aircraft to guide ships through the strait — was the week's most consequential escalation, with Iran explicitly declaring it a ceasefire violation. The fragile truce that has held since April 7 now faces its most direct test.

The diplomatic track collapsed in stages then quietly revived. Trump rejected Iran's 14-point proposal Tuesday, Rubio dismissed it Saturday insisting nuclear concessions are non-negotiable, and the IRGC declared Trump 'must choose between an impossible military operation or a bad deal.' But on Sunday, Iran confirmed receipt of a formal US written counter via Pakistan — revealing active back-channel diplomacy beneath the public posturing. The blockade's stranglehold tightened: 48 ships redirected in 20 days, $4.8B in Iranian revenue destroyed, Hormuz traffic down 90%. Spirit Airlines ceased all operations May 2 — 17,000 jobs lost after jet fuel doubled to $4.51/gallon — the war's most visible domestic economic casualty.

Israel's Lebanon campaign hit its deadliest stretch since the ceasefire: 41 killed in a single 24-hour period with 50 airstrikes across Nabatieh and Tyre districts, pushing the total past 2,659 dead. The IDF bulldozed a Catholic convent in Yaroun. Off Yemen, Somali pirates hijacked the tanker M/T Eureka — the fourth such incident in weeks — as naval forces' Hormuz distraction created a piracy surge. The Pentagon ordered 5,000 troops out of Germany; Trump promised deeper cuts. Rubio bypassed Congress on $8.6B in arms sales. In Zanjan, 14 IRGC demining specialists died. Iran executed protester Sassan Azadvar, 21.
weekly.2026-05-18:
The week opened with Iran's formal rejection of the US five-point proposal and ended with mediators converging on Tehran around a still-unsigned deal. Trump canceled a planned strike at Gulf allies' request, then gave Iran 'two or three days' to produce a deal — Vance at the podium with 'locked and loaded' language while insisting progress was real. By week's end Rubio saw 'good signs,' Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir was in Tehran and Qatar had joined the mediation, yet the bargain stayed deadlocked on two points: the fate of Iran's enriched uranium, which Tehran warned a forced handover would 'kill the deal' over, and Iran's demand to toll Hormuz traffic.

On the ground, Lebanon absorbed the war's daily violence despite the ceasefire. Israeli strikes pushed the toll past 3,100, while Hezbollah's drone campaign critically wounded the IDF's 401st Armored Brigade commander on May 20 and an army combat photographer on May 21. Inside Iran, Amnesty warned that 78 prisoners face execution amid the worst wave of political hangings since the 1980s.

The geopolitical backdrop hardened: at NATO, chiefs confronted the war's drain on Western arsenals as the US pulled 5,000 troops from Europe, while Putin and Xi signed ~40 deals and a 'multipolar world' declaration in Beijing — a reminder that every week this war runs, the Russia-China axis consolidates and American attention stays pinned on the Gulf.
weekly.2026-06-01:
The week began with diplomacy and ended with the war's worst escalation in months. A US-brokered conditional ceasefire for Lebanon collapsed on June 3-4 when Hezbollah's Naim Qassem rejected it as 'a roadmap to annihilate part of the Lebanese people,' exposing the unbridgeable gap between the Lebanese state's willingness to deal and the militia that does the fighting.

That fault line detonated on June 7. Israel struck Beirut's Dahiyeh in daylight, killing two, and Iran — which had declared the Lebanese capital a red line — answered with ballistic missiles at the Ramat David airbase, shattering the truce that had held since April 8. Iran framed it as 'a warning'; both sides paused on June 8 after roughly 30 missiles, with Iran threatening 'crushing' retaliation and Trump leaning on Netanyahu to stop or be left 'on your own.'

The pause did not hold. By week's end the Lebanon and Iran fronts had been re-fused into one escalation chain, Washington was edging back toward direct involvement, and Iran's domestic execution wave ground on — the grim backdrop to a war that kept widening.
weekly.2026-06-08:
The week opened in open warfare and closed with a signed peace on Trump's birthday. After June 8's brief mutual missile halt, the US widened its direct role: strikes on Iranian air defenses, a downed Apache over Hormuz, the fatal hit on the tanker MT Settebello that killed three Indian sailors, and Trump's threat to seize Iran's oil sector and Kharg Island. Iran declared Hormuz closed; the IAEA Board formally found Tehran non-compliant.

Then diplomacy broke through. By June 12 Pakistan said the US and Iran had agreed a 'final text'; Trump canceled planned strikes. On June 14 he declared the deal 'complete' — blockade lifted, Hormuz reopening toll-free, an immediate ceasefire 'on all fronts including Lebanon,' and a memorandum to be signed June 19 in Geneva ahead of 60 days of nuclear talks. Brent crashed below $87 and world leaders welcomed the breakthrough.

Yet the war refused to stop cleanly. Israel — never a party to the talks and warning the MOU 'endangers' its security — struck 70+ Hezbollah targets and bombed Beirut's Dahiyeh and Nabatieh on the eve of the deal, killing civilians and nearly collapsing it. Trump rebuked Netanyahu in extraordinary terms. Inside Iran, executions accelerated past 780 for 2026 as 78 Nobel laureates demanded UN intervention. Peace was declared, but not yet kept.
weekly.2026-06-15:
The week delivered the war's formal end — on paper — then spent its remaining days watching that paper nearly tear. After a digital signing on June 14-15, Trump inked a hard copy of the 14-point memorandum at a Versailles dinner on June 17, Pezeshkian signed, Tehran declared it 'in effect,' and Khamenei gave a grudging written blessing while pre-authorizing Iran's exit if Washington overreached. Shipping crept back — Iranian crude and three Saudi supertankers crossed Hormuz, backstopped by $20 billion in US reinsurance — even as the $300 billion Reconstruction Fund drew bipartisan fire, forcing Trump to deny any '$300 Billion Dollar payment.'

But the deal lived or died on Lebanon, a front Israel controls and insists it is 'not party' to. The June 19 Geneva ratification collapsed amid Israel's deadliest day — 47 killed — pulling back only when a Qatar-, US- and Iran-brokered ceasefire was struck hours later. The truce barely held: Israeli strikes killed at least 32 more on June 20 and 80-plus Hezbollah targets were hit on June 21, pushing the Lebanon toll past 4,000, while Iran retaliated by re-declaring Hormuz closed as CENTCOM insisted ships still moved.

The week closed on June 21 with implementation talks finally underway in Bürgenstock, where mediators reported 'encouraging progress' — a de-confliction cell, a Hormuz communication line and a roadmap to a final deal — even as Trump's threat to 'hit Iran very hard again' briefly froze the room. A CSIS tally put the war's cost to the Pentagon near $40 billion. A week meant to bury the war instead proved its peace is hostage to a Lebanese front no one at the table fully commands.
weekly.2026-06-29:
The week opened with the war frozen rather than ended. After the weekend's exchange — two nights of US strikes, Iranian missiles on Kuwait and Bahrain, and a dead Qatari civilian — Washington and Tehran agreed to stand down and revive talks, but the terms were contested. Delegations negotiated only indirectly through Qatari and Pakistani mediators; Iran refused a final deal until the US 'forced' Israel to halt its Lebanon strikes and warned it was 'also prepared for war.'

The economic track eased. Two days of Doha talks produced 'positive progress,' a violations hotline and a partial unfreeze of Iran's $6 billion in assets, while the Strait of Hormuz genuinely reopened — traffic rebounded from five ships a day toward a pre-war range of about 35 tankers and Brent fell to $70.78, its lowest of the war. The nuclear file moved the other way: Pezeshkian suspended IAEA cooperation, ejecting cameras and inspectors, a step Sa'ar called 'scandalous.'

The week closed on a funeral, not a battlefield, timed for America's July 4 anniversary. Iran displayed Khamenei's casket as crowds chanted 'Death to America' and held day-two prayers July 5 under a sealed Tehran airspace — yet no major power sent its top leader and successor Mojtaba stayed hidden, exposing a leadership vacuum. Trump taunted from Mount Rushmore that Washington had 'given Iran a week off,' while Russia's Medvedev likened Iran's grip on Hormuz to a 'nuclear weapon.' Even so the unwinding accelerated — Britain and France joined Oman's Hormuz demining and Iran opened oil talks with Japan — as inflation hit 88.6% and a monitor logged 141 June executions. Off Yemen, a bulk carrier came under fire near Hodeidah and Houthis mounted their deadliest assault in years — a flicker of Red Sea risk.
weekly.2026-07-06:
The week began at a funeral and ended with Iran fighting a five-front air war against the entire Gulf. July 6 brought the climactic 12-hour procession of Khamenei's coffin across Tehran, hundreds of thousands chanting for revenge as Trump vowed the US would win 'one way or the other.'

Then the truce collapsed outright. Overnight into July 7 the IRGC struck three tankers in Hormuz; the US answered with 80-plus strikes and revoked the oil-sanctions waiver anchoring the June memorandum. Iran hit US bases in Bahrain and Kuwait on July 8 as Trump declared the ceasefire 'over' at the NATO summit; a second US wave hit ~90 targets on July 9 as Tehran retaliated across four countries at once.

Washington tried an ultimatum on July 10 — declare Hormuz open and stop firing on ships by Saturday, or face 'harsh consequences.' Iran answered with force instead: on July 11 the IRGC disabled the container ship GFS Galaxy in the strait, then declared Hormuz closed 'until further notice,' asserting reopening 'rests exclusively with Iran.' CENTCOM hit back within hours, ~140 targets, pushing the week's total past 300. Iran's dawn response on July 12 hit Qatar's Al-Udeid airbase, Jordan's Prince Hassan airbase and Oman's Duqm port, injuring three civilians in Doha; CENTCOM answered by declaring the strait simply 'open,' even as real transits collapsed to 21 a day. Washington opened a second night of strikes that evening, and for the first time Iran reported a direct death on its own soil — a security guard killed at a Khuzestan water station. The week that opened with an ultimatum closed with both sides claiming the same strait and Iranian casualties finally entering the ledger.
weekly.2026-07-13:
The war's third full week of renewed fighting climbed from civilian casualties into infrastructure warfare, then spilled American blood. An IRGC strike on the US base at Azraq, Jordan killed two service members and left one missing on Saturday — the first US military deaths since March — and a third soldier died in Iraq days later, taking the war's American toll to 17. The US mounted eight-plus straight nights of strikes across Bandar Abbas, Bushehr, Tehran and Semnan, reinstated a naval blockade, and by week's end had cut water to 10,000 Iranians at the Bonji desalination plant and struck the unfinished Darkhovin nuclear site, drawing an IAEA inquiry. Iran's death toll passed 50 since June 27.

Infrastructure became the battlefield: US strikes felled six Hormozgan bridges and power sites — Iran admitting grid damage for the first time — while Iran torched two Kuwaiti desalination plants and fired on Bahrain, Jordan and Qatar's Al Udeid, downing a US MQ-9 and near-halting Hormuz traffic. The Gulf Cooperation Council branded Tehran's targeting of civilian infrastructure 'war crimes,' and the diplomatic exit closed as Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei called Trump's signature 'worthless' and Tehran suspended the June deal.

A second front simmered: the Houthis declared their Riyadh truce over, Iran readied them to shut the Red Sea, and Israel killed Hezbollah operators in south Lebanon even as President Aoun met Rubio in Washington to advance Hezbollah's disarmament. Brent held near $88–90 as Iran's wartime executions ground on, hanging January-uprising protesters through the week.
weekly.2026-07-20:
The fourth week of renewed war ran thirteen straight nights of US strikes — hitting Bushehr, Darkhovin, the Shalamcheh crossing and Iran's drone and logistics networks — before CENTCOM abruptly halted, skipping strikes two nights running in the first sustained pause since the campaign resumed. Trump cast the hold as leverage, saying he was 'not in a hurry.' Diplomacy finally moved: the AP reported both sides want back into the interim ceasefire, with talks centering on Iran policing Hormuz transit under lighter restrictions, and Iran reported progress in weekend Oman talks.

The war widened even as its core front cooled. The WSJ reported Bahrain and Kuwait had launched airstrikes into Iran under UAE air cover. The Houthis blockaded Saudi Arabia, shut Bab el-Mandeb, struck two Saudi tankers and by week's end hit land targets — Aramco's Jizan refinery and the Yanbu export hub; Saudi Arabia bombed Hodeidah in reprisal, and the Houthis fired back at the kingdom. Ukraine struck an Iranian military-cargo vessel in the Caspian, killing a sailor. Trump menaced the deep-buried Pickaxe Mountain centrifuge site; Brent broke $100 and US pump prices reached $4.11 a gallon.

At home, Hegseth put the war's cost at $37.5bn and accused Russia and China of enabling Iran — a claim Trump reversed days later. The Pentagon quietly revised the US toll to 18 killed and 624 wounded amid transparency questions. Iran rejected an Iraqi-brokered ceasefire, the House rebuked Trump a second time, and the Senate blocked the companion war-powers measure 49-47.
weekly.2026-07-27:
The fifth week of renewed war opened on a diplomatic upswing, spent itself in cross-regional escalation, and ended almost exactly where it started. CENTCOM's pause hardened into an Oman-brokered Hormuz track and Netanyahu flew to Washington; Brent cratered ~16% across three sessions. Then on July 28 the IRGC broke the lull with a surprise ballistic-missile barrage on US forces in Jordan — all intercepted — and US and Saudi jets answered within hours, killing at least 10 Iran-backed fighters in Iraq. When Iran struck again, Trump unleashed a 'heavy wave' on dozens of IRGC targets, killing a family of three on Qeshm.

The war then metastasized outward. Iran hit a US-owned LNG tanker at Egypt's Damietta port and sent drones at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain and Jordan on successive nights; unclaimed projectiles struck tankers at the mouth of Hormuz. Israel destroyed a Hezbollah tunnel network under Beaufort with 700 tons of explosives, and Saudi Arabia founded a 14-nation Red Sea alliance.

The week's real story was its ending. By August 1 Washington had readied one of the harshest bombing campaigns of the war — power plants, refineries, a possible Tehran blackout — and Israel went to its highest alert. Then, an hour after a call from the Saudi crown prince, Trump cancelled it, promising instead that talks with Iran on reopening Hormuz would begin Monday. Iran's response split: Araghchi called the Oman-mediated strait talks 'final stages,' while a spokesman insisted the waterway would never return to its pre-war status. Five weeks of ultimatum-and-reprieve have produced a Hamas disarmament roadmap Israel won't commit to — Gaza's toll still climbing past 18 on Sunday — a strait still closed at 89% below normal, and no signed deal with Tehran.
weekly.2026-08-10:
Week seven ended with the ceasefire architecture visibly dead. Politico reported the Islamabad ceasefire lapses Monday, August 17, with talks frozen over navigation rights, and Araghchi closed the week saying Tehran has made no decision to resume negotiations at all. Mohsen Rezaei, newly atop the Supreme National Security Council, authored the collapse: he decoupled the near-finished Iran-Oman lane arrangement from reopening the strait, which now stays shut until the US ends the war, lifts the blockade and releases frozen assets.

Washington answered by redefining the war as an open-ended siege - Hegseth on indefinite blockade, Bessent on "economic isolation, like the world has never seen before," Vance ranking cheap fuel above the bomb as the war's purpose. Trump's claim that he will declare Hormuz "a territory of the United States" came the same day the IRGC downed an MQ-9 over Hormozgan. The sea war stayed lethal both ways: Hellfires into the Vela Nova, a strike on the Tihamah that killed six, three ADNOC vessels hit inside a week, transits at 17 percent of pre-war volume. The UAE promised only to defend navigation "while continuing the path of dialog" - the Gulf declining the confrontation Washington is staging on its behalf.

Lebanon reheated hardest at the close. Qassem rejected disarmament as a "humiliating mistake"; a Hezbollah drone then wounded three Israeli soldiers on the Ali Taher ridge, and Israel's reprisal killed 11 across Ansar and Deir al-Zahrani, the deadliest day since the June 26 framework. Underneath sat the quietest and most damaging report of the week: Israeli defence officials say Iran is rebuilding missile production far faster than they forecast.
weekly.2026-08-17:
Week eight opened with the ceasefire architecture formally gone and closed with Washington swapping the war for a siege. The 60-day Islamabad window expired Monday with no successor - 'There's nobody to negotiate with', Trump said, while threatening to bomb Oman, the state actually brokering a Hormuz transit map. Two Iranian ballistic missiles reached UAE waters Tuesday, and Abu Dhabi became the first Gulf state to sever economic ties outright.

From Wednesday the escalation ran on money. Trump declared an 'ECONOMIC D-DAY'; Bessent gave it a goal - 'the toughest sanctions in history' as a 'one-two punch' with the blockade, explicitly to 'collapse this regime'. China, which buys over 80% of Iran's seaborne crude, replied that 'sanctions and pressure do not help'. Markets sided with escalation: Brent closed near $94, tanker charters at $500,000 a day, Hormuz transits down to 2-6 ships, and US gas hit $4.11 a gallon, the priciest August on record.

Tehran ran both tracks of its playbook at once. Pezeshkian said it was 'better to end the war today' from 'strength' while his Armed Forces chief promised 'crushing, punishing and devastating' responses; Khamenei ally Hossein Taeb dismissed Trump's threats as 'desperation'. Yet Iran's and Oman's foreign ministers discussed resuming Hormuz talks, and Tehran quietly waived the blockade for Iraqi tankers - the closure is selective, not absolute. Driving the split: a 960 trillion toman deficit and inflation above 90%, a budget official admitting 'we spent the money and the pot has reached the bottom.' Repression widened too - more Sharif University expulsions, more executions - while Beirut demanded Tehran stop meddling after Ghalibaf touted contact with Hezbollah fighters.
